title: Garry Tan on Taste, Agents and Founder Ambition

reader_summary.headline: Garry Tan shares advice on taste, AI agents, and building ambitious companies.
reader_summary.overview: Garry Tan argues founders should follow their unique interests rather than chasing trends. He explains how AI agents allow small teams to build massive products quickly by automating work and fixing bugs automatically. He also suggests solving local community problems is the best way to create real change.

key_points.text: Founders should follow their unique knowledge instead of chasing what is currently popular.
key_points.evidence_quote: The right question is, what are you interested in? What do you know uniquely? And so that's one of a great many mistakes I made in my career.

key_points.text: New tools like AI coding agents mean one person can now do the work of many, changing how teams are built.
key_points.evidence_quote: literally any given person could be 400 of that person, like from two years, like even like nine months ago, you can be a multiple of yourself.

key_points.text: Success no longer depends on chasing old metrics like SaaS revenue multiples, but on building new advantages like data or network effects.
key_points.evidence_quote: if you're doing that now in 2026, like, you better hope that that's, like, a leap to some sort of moat around data or network effects or something else.

key_points.text: Agents help manage conflict by looking at data and meeting transcripts instead of relying on human emotions.
key_points.evidence_quote: He can use meetings that he's not in to figure out like what's broken, what's in conflict. Like who's in conflict with who?

key_points.text: Act local to solve immediate community needs like housing and crime rather than focusing only on national goals.
key_points.evidence_quote: And so yeah, act local, like take care of the people right next to you. Like, you know, I think it's funny, so many people get very, very obsessed with national.

thesis: The episode argues that founders should stop chasing what is currently hot and instead follow what they uniquely know and are interested in, drawing on Garry Tan's experience of regretting his early career moves where he followed trends rather than his own expertise. It further suggests that the most interesting opportunities in Silicon Valley often come from the fringe or intellectual edges rather than the mainstream, and that founders should trust their direct experience over consensus or external contradictions.
